title: Mindfulness Meditation
body:
Mindfulness meditation, as practiced in Buddhist traditions and in secular adaptations, is the practice of attending to the present moment, breath, body, and thoughts without judgment, usually seated, for minutes to an hour at a time.

Documented practice: practitioners describe calmer attention, reduced reactivity, and a clearer sense of their own thoughts, and researchers study attention and stress measures in meditators, with results that vary and do not establish supernatural effects. Believers in some traditions describe meditation as a path toward insight, compassion, and, in the fullest accounts, liberation from suffering.

Faith-based framing: any extraordinary abilities described as arising from meditation are reported within those traditions as fruits of long practice, not as demonstrated physical powers. This record is labeled faith-based throughout: it describes what practitioners and believers report and practice, as documented belief and practice, never as a proven physical mechanism, and it contains no preaching and no invitation to convert.

title: Intercessory Prayer
body:
Intercessory prayer is the practice of praying on behalf of others, asking a divine being for healing, help, protection, or guidance for someone other than the pray-er, common in Christian, Jewish, Muslim, and other traditions.

Documented practice: believers describe prayer as communion, as trust, and as a way of carrying others' burdens, and communities organize prayer chains, lists, and gatherings for the sick and the suffering. Researchers study health outcomes in prayed-for groups with mixed and contested results, and no study establishes prayer as a physical mechanism.

Faith-based framing: healings and interventions attributed to prayer are reported by believers as divine action, not as demonstrated physical causation. title: Religious Fasting
body:
Religious fasting is the practice of abstaining from food, drink, or both for a set time as a spiritual discipline, observed in Ramadan, Lent, Yom Kippur, and many other traditions, each with its own rules and exemptions.

Documented practice: practitioners describe fasting as purification, self-discipline, solidarity with the poor, and closeness to God, and traditions exempt the sick, the young, the pregnant, and travelers. Health researchers study fasting's metabolic effects separately from its spiritual meanings, and the two are not the same claim.

Faith-based framing: spiritual benefits and any extraordinary experiences reported during fasting are described within the traditions as religious, not as proven physical powers. title: Yoga as Spiritual Discipline
body:
Yoga as a spiritual discipline, in its Hindu roots and in many modern adaptations, joins posture, breath control, and meditation as a path toward self-knowledge, discipline, and, in classical accounts, liberation.

Documented practice: practitioners describe flexibility, strength, calm, and concentration as fruits of practice, and researchers study yoga's effects on stress, balance, and pain with modest, variable results. Classical texts describe advanced attainments, called siddhis, as byproducts of deep practice that the practitioner is warned not to pursue for their own sake.

title: Tai Chi as Meditative Movement
body:
Tai chi, rooted in Chinese martial and Daoist traditions, is slow, flowing movement joined with breath and attention, practiced in parks and halls as health exercise, martial art, and meditation at once.

Documented practice: practitioners describe balance, calm, and bodily awareness as fruits of practice, and researchers study tai chi's effects on balance, falls in older adults, and stress with generally positive but modest results. Traditions describe internal energy, qi, as cultivated by the practice, a concept from Chinese philosophy and medicine, not a measured physical force.

title: Vision Quest (as Described in Some Indigenous Traditions)
body:
A vision quest, as described in some Indigenous North American traditions, is a period of solitude, fasting, and prayer in nature, undertaken to seek guidance, a vision, or a life direction, under the guidance of elders and within a community's protocols.

Documented practice: the quest is described by its peoples as a sacred, communal responsibility, not a solitary adventure, and its protocols, timing, and interpretation belong to the specific community, which outsiders are expected to respect rather than imitate casually. Anthropologists document quests as social and religious facts, distinct from the spiritual claims made within them.

Faith-based framing: visions and guidance received on a quest are reported within the traditions as spiritual experience, not as demonstrated physical mechanisms.
